READING

**Dead mileage penalty**

Culverstone is three miles further each way to the Verrancombe Bridge stand. Each of the 22 vehicles makes at least one outward dead run and one return dead run per operating day.

Extra miles per year: 22 × 313 × 6 = 41,316 miles
Extra cost at £0.63: £26,029 per year

Net annual rent saving, KESTERWICK over ARDENSHAW: £96,000 − £26,029 = **£69,971 ≈ £70,000**

**Capital account**

| Item | £ |
|---|---|
| Faskally deposit (December) | 40,000 |
| Culverstone works | 480,000 |
| Total committed capital | **520,000** |

Cash after outlay: £640,000 − £520,000 = £120,000 remaining, plus the £200,000 undrawn facility. The works will draw over approximately five months, so the cash curve is not a cliff. Even adding a worst-case Nethercote stint (see below) the business stays solvent.

**Payback**

At £70,000 net saving per year: £520,000 ÷ £70,000 = **7.4 years**. The investment is recovered inside the ten-year term with roughly 2.5 years of clear benefit before the lease rolls again. ARDENSHAW forfeits all of that.

**Planning scenarios — when does Culverstone open?**

The application was validated 2026-08-14. The lease at Hallowbrand expires 2027-11-30.

| Scenario | Consent granted | Build complete (+22 wks) | Ahead of Hallowbrand expiry? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Target (13 wks) | 2026-11-12 | 2027-04-08 | Yes, 7½ months |
| Median (34 wks) | 2027-04-08 | 2027-09-10 | Yes, 2½ months |
| Slowest on record (61 wks) | 2027-10-14 | 2028-03-18 | No — gap of ~3½ months |

In the median case (the most representative expectation), Culverstone opens in early September 2027 and Hallowbrand expires in late November 2027 — no gap, no Nethercote.

In the worst-recorded case, the gap is roughly 3½ months on Nethercote: 3.5 × £18,500 ≈ **£65,000**, plus the operational friction of running 31 vehicles with no workshop. Painful and worth planning for, but bounded. The Faskally deposit (paid in December 2026) holds the site until 2028-06-30, which covers even the worst planning outcome with four months to spare.

**The September 2027 contract bid**

This is where the two courses diverge most sharply. The 44/44A bid is due 2027-09-14. Depot cost enters as a fixed line.

Under ARDENSHAW: the fixed line is £214,000. Certain, but large.

Under KESTERWICK:
- Median scenario: Culverstone occupied ~2027-09-10, four days before the bid. Depot cost priced at £118,000 + ~£26,000 dead mileage = £144,000.
- Worst-case scenario: at bid date, planning has not yet been granted (consent expected ~2027-10-14). However, the new contract does not start until 2028-04-01. In the slowest planning case, Culverstone is ready ~2028-03-18 — just in time. A bidder in that position can legitimately price Culverstone for the contract period, carrying the residual consent risk explicitly in their risk register.

The bid-cost difference is £70,000 per year. Over a typical contract term of three to five years that is £210,000–£350,000 of structural cost advantage in the tender. In a competitively scored procurement where depot cost is a transparent fixed line, this matters enormously. ARDENSHAW does not merely cost more to operate — it costs more to bid, potentially for every future tender cycle until 2037.

**Worst-case scenario integrity check**

If planning takes the full 61 weeks and Culverstone is not ready until March 2028:
- Trentmoor is on Nethercote from approximately 2027-12-01 to 2028-03-18 (≈ 3½ months)
- Nethercote cost: ≈ £65,000
- No workshop: maintenance must be subcontracted or vehicles sent out; this adds cost and risk but does not stop operations
- Bid submitted Sept 2027 with consent not yet granted: a legitimate commercial risk to carry; the depot option is held by the deposit and the contract start date gives breathing room
- Total worst-case outlay: £520,000 capital + £65,000 Nethercote ≈ £585,000, still within cash plus facility (£840,000 available)

**Planning refusal — the real tail risk**

The one scenario that breaks KESTERWICK entirely is refusal of consent. In that event, the Hallowbrand offer deadline (2026-12-19) has passed, the £40,000 deposit is gone, and Trentmoor is on Nethercote indefinitely seeking a third site. This is a genuine risk. It is also the question management must answer before committing: is there a material ground for refusal? The figures given do not suggest one (it is a commercial depot development going through a slow but functioning planning authority), and Aurelio has not flagged it as a concern. Treated as a low-probability event, it does not override the financial arithmetic, but it is the one condition that reverses the recommendation.

**Summary comparison**

| | KESTERWICK | ARDENSHAW |
|---|---|---|
| Annual rent | £118,000 | £214,000 |
| Dead mileage penalty | £26,000 | £0 |
| Net annual cost | £144,000 | £214,000 |
| Annual saving vs alternative | +£70,000 | — |
| Capital required | £520,000 | £0 |
| Payback period | 7.4 years | n/a |
| 10-year net benefit over alternative | ≈ +£180,000 (before worst-case Nethercote) | — |
| Workshop | New two-bay | Existing |
| Bid cost (Sept 2027) | £144,000 | £214,000 |
| Planning/consent risk | Yes — bounded worst case | None |
| Cash remaining after commitment | ~£120,000 + £200k facility | Unchanged |

KESTERWICK is not a comfortable slam-dunk: the ten-year margin after recovering capital is around £100,000–£180,000 depending on Nethercote exposure, and the planning timeline creates genuine operational tension around both the lease break and the bid date. But every scenario short of outright refusal lands better than ARDENSHAW, and the bid arithmetic — £70,000 a year of fixed cost advantage in a competitively tendered network that puts 22 of 31 vehicles to work — is the factor that makes the choice clear.

---

READING
  Culverstone saves £70,000 net per year after dead mileage, repaying the £520,000 capital outlay in 7.4 years and leaving roughly £180,000 of net benefit inside the ten-year term even in the worst Nethercote scenario. The median planning outcome (consent April 2027, occupation September 2027) delivers the site before Hallowbrand expires with no gap; the worst recorded outcome creates a bounded 3½-month Nethercote stint that is affordable from cash. Critically, pricing the September 2027 bid at an effective depot cost of £144,000 rather than £214,000 gives Trentmoor a £70,000-a-year structural advantage on the fixed line that decides competitiveness for the 44/44A contract — the revenue backbone of the operation. Planning refusal is the single scenario that breaks this logic; absent a material ground for refusal, the financial and competitive case for Culverstone is decisive.

CALL
  KESTERWICK

GROUNDS
  The £70,000 annual net saving after dead mileage recovers the capital within the ten-year term with years to spare, and pricing the September 2027 bid at £144,000 against a competitor who has signed at Hallowbrand for £214,000 protects the revenue stream on which thirty-one vehicles depend more decisively than any rent-certainty argument can answer.
